item.title: Golden Hour in Jefferson
item.description: There's a quiet road in Jefferson, NH with an expansive view of the northern Presidential Range, no hiking required. Here's a close up of Mt. Jefferson and Mt. Washington from the side of the road.
item.content:encoded:
There's a quiet road in Jefferson, NH with an expansive view of the northern Presidential Range, no hiking required. Here's a close up of Mt. Jefferson and Mt. Washington from the side of the road.

Because this spot is on the broad plain of the Israel River valley, you can also see Mt. Madison (left, in shade) and Mt. Adams.

Wait ten minutes and the sun drops below the horizon. The light changes. Golden hour has shifted to blue.

item.title: Lower Montalban Ridge
item.description: Montalban Ridge extends south from Mt. Washington over Boott Spur and Mt. Isolation. After Stairs Mountain, the ridge splits into two arms -- one continuing south over Mt. Crawford; the other tacking east over Mt. Resolution, Mt. Parker, and on to Mt. Stanton. These photos are from the Mt. Stanton Trail, a very pleasant walk over the rocky spine of the lower ridge.
item.content:encoded:
Montalban Ridge extends south from Mt. Washington over Boott Spur and Mt. Isolation. After Stairs Mountain, the ridge splits into two arms -- one continuing south over Mt. Crawford; the other tacking east over Mt. Resolution, Mt. Parker, and on to Mt. Stanton. These photos are from the Mt. Stanton Trail, a very pleasant walk over the rocky spine of the lower ridge.

Mt. Stanton Trail offers views of neighboring peaks from several outlooks. Here's Iron Mountain just north of Mt. Stanton.

And further north is Carter Notch. On the east side of the notch, Carter Dome is already touched by snow and ice.

Since Mt. Stanton Trail never rises above 2400 feet, it will be a while before winter sets in. There's still time to appreciate sights like this juniper hugging a sunny ledge and bursting with berries.

item.title: Snyder Brook
item.description: Snyder Brook, in Randolph, runs roughly parallel to Valley Way. The Fallsway and Brookbank trails hug the edges of Snyder Brook and feature views of many waterfalls, making either trail a great alternative to the lower section of Valley Way.
item.content:encoded:
Snyder Brook, in Randolph, runs roughly parallel to Valley Way. The Fallsway and Brookbank trails hug the edges of Snyder Brook and feature views of many waterfalls, making either trail a great alternative to the lower section of Valley Way.

Here's Tama Fall, just off Brookbank.

Upper Salroc Falls.

Gordon Fall.

And these are just the waterfalls with names. There are many unnamed rills and falls along Snyder Brook too.

item.title: Church Pond
item.description: Church Pond is a little more than a mile off the Kancamagus Highway, but it feels much more remote. The usual route to the pond is from Camp Passaconaway via the Church Pond Loop Trail. While this used to be a loop, the east section of the trail is permanently closed, now making it an out-and-back route.
item.content:encoded:
Church Pond is a little more than a mile off the Kancamagus Highway, but it feels much more remote. The usual route to the pond is from Camp Passaconaway via the Church Pond Loop Trail. While this used to be a loop, the east section of the trail is permanently closed, now making it an out-and-back route.

After walking over bog bridges through a beautiful marsh, you arrive at a knoll on the east side of the pond. Follow one of the herd paths down to the shore for some great views especially to the southwest. Here is a dramatic view of Mt. Potash (left) rising on the other side of the Kancamagus Highway. To the right of Mt. Potash is the valley of Sabbaday Brook with the Sleepers in the distance.

Swing to the right just a little and North Tripyramid comes into view.

Although it's definitely past peak foliage, the tamaracks are almost neon yellow this time of year.

Tamaracks are common in New Hampshire, but they almost never dominate the landscape. It's always a pleasant surprise to catch the tamarack show after most hardwoods have dropped their leaves.

item.title: Zealand Notch
item.description: Low clouds hanging over Zealand Notch make for vibrant early fall foliage. Here is a view across Zealand Pond toward Mt. Hale.
item.content:encoded:
Low clouds hanging over Zealand Notch make for vibrant early fall foliage. Here is a view across Zealand Pond toward Mt. Hale.

Another view of the pond further up Zealand Trail.

The colors are especially brilliant around Zealand Falls Hut. This is from the top of Zealand Falls.

item.title: Guinea Pond
item.description: Guinea Pond is located in the Sandwich Range Wilderness, just south of Sandwich Mountain. Black Mountain, a subpeak of Sandwich Mountain, looms over the pond.
item.content:encoded:
Guinea Pond is located in the Sandwich Range Wilderness, just south of Sandwich Mountain. Black Mountain, a subpeak of Sandwich Mountain, looms over the pond.

To the right of Black Mountain is Sandwich Dome, the true summit of Sandwich Mountain.

Zooming out a bit, you can see how truly massive Sandwich Mountain is. From this angle, it looks like an entire mountain range, but geographically speaking, it is a single mountain.

item.title: Mt. Success
item.description: Imagine you are hiking the Appalachian Trail northbound. You are almost finished with New Hampshire. You just have one more climb -- Mt. Success. As you near the summit, you look south to see some of the mountains you have already traveled over, the Carter-Moriah Range and the Northern Presidentials.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine you are hiking the Appalachian Trail northbound. You are almost finished with New Hampshire. You just have one more climb -- Mt. Success. As you near the summit, you look south to see some of the mountains you have already traveled over, the Carter-Moriah Range and the Northern Presidentials.

You push north over bog bridges to the summit of Mt. Success.

From there, you get your first proper look at Goose Eye and the mountains of Maine.

item.title: Flat Mountain Pond
item.description: Flat Mountain Pond is a remote, upland pond in the Sandwich Range Wilderness. It's accessible only on foot by the Flat Mountain Pond Trail. This is a view of Sandwich Mountain from the north shore of the pond.
item.content:encoded:
Flat Mountain Pond is a remote, upland pond in the Sandwich Range Wilderness. It's accessible only on foot by the Flat Mountain Pond Trail. This is a view of Sandwich Mountain from the north shore of the pond.

On the south side of the pond there are a few designated camp sites and lots of evidence of an old logging camp. This is what remains of an old dam at the source of Pond Brook.

The south side also has some terrific views across the pond toward the Tripyramids, the Sleepers, and Mt. Whiteface.

item.title: Monadnock Summit Bog
item.description: There are many microclimates scattered around the summit of Mt. Monadnock. It's fascinating to return to a favorite spot at different times of the year. This bog is just below the summit on Pumpelly Trail. Today, the bog is full of spring green foliage.
item.content:encoded:
There are many microclimates scattered around the summit of Mt. Monadnock. It's fascinating to return to a favorite spot at different times of the year. This bog is just below the summit on Pumpelly Trail. Today, the bog is full of spring green foliage.

Later this summer, the bog cotton will emerge to dance in the wind (photo from August, 2024).

Autumn brings deep, rusty tones (photo from October, 2023).

And the long winter above 3000 feet is almost entirely black and white (photo from November, 2025).

item.title: Chocorua in the Clouds
item.description: The summit of Mt. Chocorua is often crowded with hikers. Apparently, unsettled weather keeps the crowds at bay. It is a rare treat to have the summit to yourself.
item.content:encoded:
The summit of Mt. Chocorua is often crowded with hikers. Apparently, unsettled weather keeps the crowds at bay. It is a rare treat to have the summit to yourself.

Even though the clouds cover most neighboring peaks, North Tripyramid might make an appearance.

And it is magical walking along the exposed section of Piper Trail.

item.title: Monadnock Summit Engravings
item.description: Henry David Thoreau visited Mt. Monadnock on four separate occasions. As he wrote in his journal, he wasn't a fan of noisy tourists:
item.content:encoded:
Henry David Thoreau visited Mt. Monadnock on four separate occasions. As he wrote in his journal, he wasn't a fan of noisy tourists:

Indeed this peak in pleasant weather is the most trivial place in New England - there are prob. more arrivals daily than at any of the white mt houses. Several were busily engraving their names on the rock with cold chisels - whose incessant chink you heard - & they had but little leisure to look off.

Apparently, the noise started long before Thoreau got there. P.S. Grant made his mark in 1808.

H.J. Brown made his mark several years later. (Brown may not have been a tourist. As indicated by his engraving, he may have been associated with the USGS, but I haven't been able to verify that.)

At some point in the 20th century, tourists stopped (or where prohibited from) chiseling the summit rocks. It's good thing. Imagine the summit with more engravings than there already are.

item.title: Artist's Bluff
item.description: Artist's Bluff is an outlook on the north end of Franconia Notch. In the past few years, it has become "Instagram famous". On a fine day in early October, it is standing room only.
item.content:encoded:
Artist's Bluff is an outlook on the north end of Franconia Notch. In the past few years, it has become "Instagram famous". On a fine day in early October, it is standing room only.

There were no crowds on the bluff today.

Here is the same view in October of 2016.

I avoid Artist's Bluff and the crowds in the fall, but I understand the appeal. It's a quick, easy hike with a fantastic view. Just remember, the view is there all year round.

item.title: Moats Traverse
item.description: The Moat Mountain Range is just west of North Conway. If you enjoy a ridge walk on open ledges, the Moats Traverse is good choice this time of year. It's less crowded than Franconia Ridge, and because they are lower in elevation, the Moats offer a better view of the foliage in the valleys. Here's a look at Mt. Chocorua from South Moat.
item.content:encoded:
The Moat Mountain Range is just west of North Conway. If you enjoy a ridge walk on open ledges, the Moats Traverse is good choice this time of year. It's less crowded than Franconia Ridge, and because they are lower in elevation, the Moats offer a better view of the foliage in the valleys. Here's a look at Mt. Chocorua from South Moat.

This is the view north from Middle Moat. That's North Moat on the right.

And here's a view from North Moat. Crawford Notch is on the left, Mt. Washington is just right of center, and Carter Notch is on the right.

item.title: Mt. Clay
item.description: Mt. Clay is the "little" mountain to the right of Mt. Washington. It's 5525 feet above sea level, but it's not on the NH48 list because it's less than 200 feet above the low point (the col) between Washington and itself.
item.content:encoded:
Mt. Clay is the "little" mountain to the right of Mt. Washington. It's 5525 feet above sea level, but it's not on the NH48 list because it's less than 200 feet above the low point (the col) between Washington and itself.

Although it's just off the Appachian Trail, hikers and backpackers often skip Mt. Clay. Big mistake.

The Great Gulf is the huge ravine separating Mt. Washington from the northern half of the Presidential Range. Here's a view of the Great Gulf from near the summit of Mt. Clay.

North of the summit, you can see Jefferson (left), Adams and Madison. Mt. Clay is a perfect perch to pass the time on a fair weather day.

item.title: Castle Ravine
item.description: Castle Ravine is a glacial cirque on the north side of Mt. Jefferson. Here's a view down the ravine from Castle Ravine Trail.
item.content:encoded:
Castle Ravine is a glacial cirque on the north side of Mt. Jefferson. Here's a view down the ravine from Castle Ravine Trail.

On the west side of the ravine is Castellated Ridge with it's dramatic rock formations or "castles". That's Cherry Mountain just beyond the lower castle.

And on the east side of the ravine is Israel Ridge.

The main trails around the ravine are Castle Trail, Castle Ravine Trail, and Israel Ridge Trail. You can combine the main trails with various connecting trails to make many interesting routes.

item.title: North of Lafayette
item.description: The Franconia Ridge is very popular -- especially between Little Haystack and Mt. Lafayette. Day hikers are less inclined to venture north of Mt. Lafayette, but it's just as beautiful. This is Garfield Ridge Trail just north of Lafayette.
item.content:encoded:
The Franconia Ridge is very popular -- especially between Little Haystack and Mt. Lafayette. Day hikers are less inclined to venture north of Mt. Lafayette, but it's just as beautiful. This is Garfield Ridge Trail just north of Lafayette.

Further north, Mt. Garfield comes into view.

And here's a closer look at Garfield with some Labrador Tea blooming in the foreground.

item.title: Alpine Garden
item.description: The Alpine Garden is an area above treeline on Mt. Washington's eastern slope between Tuckerman Ravine and Huntington Ravine. It's a place where several varieties of alpine plants produce flowers in June and into July. June 9 is early for the flowers of some varieties, but Lapland Rosebay (pink) and Diapensia (white) are blooming on the edge of Tuckerman Ravine.
item.content:encoded:
The Alpine Garden is an area above treeline on Mt. Washington's eastern slope between Tuckerman Ravine and Huntington Ravine. It's a place where several varieties of alpine plants produce flowers in June and into July. June 9 is early for the flowers of some varieties, but Lapland Rosebay (pink) and Diapensia (white) are blooming on the edge of Tuckerman Ravine.

The high winds of the Alpine Garden cause the stunted trees to twist into strange shapes or Krummholz.

Despite the difficult conditions, Alpine Azalea is thriving. This plant is in a little nook on the leeward side of a small rock.

And there are large patches of Diapensia and Lapland Rosebay everywhere you look.

item.title: Red Hill
item.description: Red Hill in Moultonborough is a pleasant winter hike. The summit is mostly tree covered, but there are good views from the top of the fire tower.
item.content:encoded:
Red Hill in Moultonborough is a pleasant winter hike. The summit is mostly tree covered, but there are good views from the top of the fire tower.

Although getting to the summit can be warm work, you need to bundle up before climbing the steps of the tower. This is especially true on a windy day.

You are rewarded by this view of Squam Lakes to the west.

And to the northeast, is the unmistakeable shape of Mt. Chocorua .

Those are just two examples. The tower offers more views at almost every point of the compass.

item.title: Mountain View Farm
item.description: The Daniel Doan Trail is a little-used route to the summit of Smarts Mountain. The trailhead is close to Mountain View Farm in Quinttown, a section of Orford, New Hampshire.
item.content:encoded:
The Daniel Doan Trail is a little-used route to the summit of Smarts Mountain. The trailhead is close to Mountain View Farm in Quinttown, a section of Orford, New Hampshire.

The fields of Mountain View Farm offer views of the surrounding hills including Mt. Cube.

Smarts Mountain is on the 52 with a View (NH52WAV) list, but most hikers take a different route to the summit. It's a shame. If more people knew about Mountain View Farm, the Daniel Doan Trail might be more popular.

item.title: Moosilauke South Peak
item.description: Mt. Moosilauke is massive. In addition to the main summit commonly sought by NH48 peak baggers, it has three subpeaks over 4000 feet: Mt. Jim, Mt. Blue, and South Peak. These subpeaks are sometimes overlooked because they lack the prominence required by the NH48 list, but South Peak in particular has some great views.
item.content:encoded:
Mt. Moosilauke is massive. In addition to the main summit commonly sought by NH48 peak baggers, it has three subpeaks over 4000 feet: Mt. Jim, Mt. Blue, and South Peak. These subpeaks are sometimes overlooked because they lack the prominence required by the NH48 list, but South Peak in particular has some great views.

You reach South Peak by a short spur at the junction of Glencliff Trail and Moosilauke Carriage Road. Here's a view looking northwest from South Peak. That's Black Mountain just right of center on the horizon.

Swing to the northeast and the main summit of Moosilauke comes into view.

Back to the northwest, here's a view of the Tunnel Brook valley between Moosilauke and Mt. Clough.
